more_info.banned_in:
Approved in the EU.
No current country-wide food-use ban was confirmed in the regulatory sources checked in 2026.
The permissions checked in 2026 apply only to the specified preparations, food uses and conditions.
The EU rules checked in 2026 prohibit this additive in jelly mini-cups intended to be swallowed in a single bite; this is a restriction on that food format, not a ban on all authorised uses.
The EU rules checked in 2026 also prohibit its use in dehydrated foods intended to rehydrate on ingestion.
more_info.overview: Locust bean gum is the ground seed endosperm of the carob tree; its main carbohydrate is a galactomannan polysaccharide. Its emulsifying role is to help form or maintain mixtures of oil and water in the finished food. Made by grinding the endosperm inside carob seeds. The main component is a galactomannan polysaccharide. The specified material is supplied as white powder. It dissolves in hot water under the specified test conditions.
more_info.uses:
Examples in the EU food-use list include certain cocoa and Chocolate products as covered by Directive 2000/36/EC; other confectionery including breath freshening microsweets; chewing gum; decorations, coatings and fillings, except fruit-based fillings covered by category 4.2.4; fruit juices as defined by Directive 2001/112/EC and vegetable juices; flavoured fermented milk products including heat-treated products.
The entries apply to particular food categories and may limit the amount, the preparation or the way it is used; they do not show how often the additive appears in retail products.
more_info.daily_intake: No numerical ADI needed for the assessed general-population uses (EFSA, 2017).
more_info.origin: Made by grinding the endosperm inside carob seeds. The main component is a galactomannan polysaccharide.
more_info.dietary_restrictions: The specified starting material is plant derived and compatible with vegetarian and vegan diets. The specification does not establish halal or kosher certification.
more_info.side_effects:
EFSA found no concern for general-population food uses in 2017.
That assessment identified insufficient evidence for medically vulnerable infants; its conclusion should not be extended to every infant formula.
